narration: The Frog-Legged Court Craze
This is Canary dance. 16th–17th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is rooted in the indigenous traditions of the Canary Islands, and is possibly related to the Tajaraste. It crossed to mainland Spain via enslaved people by 1552, where Diego Pisador noted it at funeral feasts.

By the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, it captivated French, Italian, English, and Spanish courts, appearing in plays by William Shakespeare and dance manuals by Thoinot Arbeau in 1589, Fabritio Caroso in 1600, and Cesare Negri in 1602.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance initially functions as a lively ballroom diversion or theatrical interlude within masques, framed around the dramaturgical theme of the sauvage or indigenous wooing.
Spanish sources like Covarrubias note its lineage from saltarello-style island dances, while contemporaries relish its bizarre, high-energy spectacle.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Choreographed primarily for a single couple, early versions feature rapid heel-and-toe stamps, deep jumps, and violent movements that earn it the nickname frogs legs. Unlike the rigid court steps of the galliarde, dancers engage in free improvisation meant to mimic a playful sauvage indigenous courtship.
By the seventeenth century in France, it incorporates elaborate cabrioles, turns, and battus in a fast ternary meter.
Watch for the heel-and-toe stamp and the frogs legs jump.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Early descriptions like Arbeau's noted simple meters, while Baroque interpretations embraced fast 3/4, 6/8, and dotted rhythms akin to a rapid gigue.
Girolamo Kapsberger wrote a famous 1640 virtuoso piece for chitarrone over a three-note basso ostinato, and Gaspar Sanz published a popular version for the Spanish baroque guitar in 1674.
Listen for the chitarrone, Spanish baroque guitar, strings/violin, lute.
The pulse is binary (early) or ternary 3/4, 6/8, 6/4 (Baroque).
A rapid, driving instrumental movement driven by sharp, short bow strokes or plucked strings, defined by an energetic dotted rhythm and an insistent repeating melodic or bass cell.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dance masters Thoinot Arbeau, Fabritio Caroso, Cesare Negri, Livio Lupi da Caravaggio, and Juan de Esquivel Navarro document its steps.
Baroque composers including Girolamo Kapsberger, Gaspar Sanz, J.S. Bach, Henry Purcell, and Jean-Baptiste Lully cement its rhythmic profile.

The form manifests across Europe with distinct local flavors, including Spanish guitar adaptations by Gaspar Sanz, Italian theatrical balletto sequences by Negri and Caroso, and refined French baroque variations emphasizing brilliant footwork and rapid tempos.
It is rooted in Canary Islands indigenous movement traditions such as the Tajaraste, influences Baroque suite movements, and shares structural affinities with the gigue and saltarello.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: The Canary dance is a variant of the gigue. It is often compared to the gigue, though considered faster and sharper in execution.
The Canary dance is a variant of the saltarello. Covarrubias describes the Canary dance as a type of saltarello originating from the Canary Islands.
